title.title: Is federal contract money going to fewer companies?
title.subtitle:
Market concentration in civilian agency contracts, FY2008 to FY2025
Suchitra Hole, Shivram Nekkanti, Andy Hannah
title.notes: Our project measures market concentration in federal contracting: when the government buys something, does the money go to many companies or to a few? We look at every civilian agency, every product and every year from FY2008 to FY2025.

why.title: What concentration is, and why it matters
risks: Less pressure on the winner at renewal
No ready alternative if it fails
Rivals lose the people and know-how
One failure hits the whole market
why.takeaway: Concentration is not wrongdoing: some work only one firm can do. It is a risk worth measuring.
why.notes: Market concentration means a few companies win most of a market's money. Figure 1 shows two markets with the same budget and five companies. On the left the money is shared evenly. On the right, one company gets 80 percent. Why does it matter? Over time the winner faces less price pressure. The government depends on one supplier. Rivals drift away, so fewer firms can bid next time. And if that one company fails, the whole market is affected. But a concentrated market is not wrongdoing: only one shipyard can build an aircraft carrier. That is why we measure it carefully.

question.title: Our question: where does civilian contract money go?
points: How much goes to markets a few companies dominate?
For every civilian agency, product and year
Is that share growing, and is the growth real?
Agencies, companies and the policies behind them
question.takeaway: Defense has a handful of prime contractors and studies its own market. The civilian agencies have no such measure, so we built one.
question.notes: In FY2025 the government spent about 301 billion dollars on civilian contracts, and 492 billion on Defense. Defense buys from a handful of large weapons makers and already studies its own market, so we focus on the civilian agencies. Our three questions: how much civilian money goes to markets that a few companies dominate, whether that share is growing for real, and where, who and why.

terms.title: Key terms used in this talk
cards: A concentration score from 0 (money spread out) to 10,000 (one company has it all)
One agency buying one kind of product in one year
A segment whose HHI is above 2,500
October 1 to September 30. FY2025 ended on September 30, 2025
Every federal agency except the Department of Defense (DoD)
The company the government signs the contract with directly
Other companies could bid / one company was chosen directly
Congress's auditor. It publishes the official yearly contract totals
terms.takeaway: These terms come up on every slide that follows.
terms.notes: Before the data, the key terms. HHI stands for the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index, named after the economists Orris Herfindahl and Albert Hirschman. It is the standard measure of market concentration that the U.S. Justice Department and the Federal Trade Commission use to review mergers. It runs from near 0, money spread across many companies, to 10,000, one company with everything. A segment, or market, is one agency buying one kind of product in one year. Highly concentrated means an HHI above 2,500. A fiscal year runs October to September. Civilian agencies are everything except Defense. The data records the prime contractor, the company the government signs with directly. Competed means others could bid, and sole source means one company was chosen directly. GAO is the Government Accountability Office, Congress's auditor.

data.title: The data: every federal contract action since FY2008
data.source: Source: USAspending.gov Award Data Archive, all agencies, contracts, release of 2026-09-06.
data.takeaway: Each row says who bought what, from whom, for how much, and whether others could bid. That is all the measure needs.
data.notes: We downloaded the government's public archive: 18 yearly files, 88.8 million rows, 10.5 trillion dollars. Each row is one contract action. Here is a real one from July 2025: Veterans Affairs paid Optum, part of UnitedHealth Group, 857 million dollars for managed healthcare, and the contract was openly competed. We will come back to this market.

process.title: How we turned 18 zip files into a trusted dataset
process.takeaway: Every number traces back to the published files, and the totals agree with the government's official figures.
process.notes: Four steps. One: we checked every file against its digital fingerprint and locked it. Two: we converted 88.8 million rows to a fast format, and two independent programs agree on the row count, the dollars to the cent and every field. Three: 62 quality rules ran on every row, looking for duplicates, bad dates, placeholder names and outliers. Four: we added the rows up into 7.85 million company-by-market totals, and 116 checks confirm they add back. Our yearly totals match GAO's official figures within 0.2 percent.

cleaning.title: Why cleaning matters: one entry can fake a monopoly
issues: A $13.9B entry reversed the next year
Two $10B rows that are contract ceilings
One placeholder name for many foreign firms
A placeholder funding agency, FY2008 to FY2010
cleaning.takeaway: Without cleaning, one bad entry makes a market of 1,039 companies look like a monopoly.
cleaning.notes: Here is what the quality checks catch. In FY2008 the Army recorded a 13.9 billion dollar entry for Emerson Construction, which it reversed the next year. The real contract was about 16 million dollars. With the entry, Emerson looks like it holds 65 percent of a market of 1,039 companies, and the market scores 4,282, highly concentrated. Net the entry against its reversal and Emerson holds a fraction of a percent, and the market scores 167, very competitive. We found five issues like this, and the team's proposed rules handle each one.

segment.title: How we measure: one market at a time
segment.takeaway: A segment is one market: one buyer, one kind of product, one year. Above 2,500, the market is highly concentrated.
segment.notes: We measure concentration market by market. A segment is one agency buying one kind of product in one year. For example: Veterans Affairs buying managed healthcare in FY2025, where 75 companies shared 22.8 billion dollars. There are about 365 thousand segments in 18 years. Each gets a score, the HHI, from 0 to 10,000. Below 1,500 is competitive, 1,500 to 2,500 is moderate, and above 2,500 is highly concentrated, the bands the Justice Department and FTC use for mergers. Our VA example scores 9,680, near the top.

hhi.title: The Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI), worked through
hhi.takeaway: Squaring makes big shares count much more: one company with 98% scores almost 10,000 on its own.
hhi.notes: HHI stands for the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index. Here is the calculation. Take each company's share of the money, square it, and add them up. Five equal companies: 20 squared is 400, times five is 2,000. One company with 80 percent: 80 squared is 6,400, plus four times 5 squared, 100, gives 6,500. On the right is a real market from our data, VA managed healthcare in FY2025. UnitedHealth Group had 98.39 percent: squared, that is 9,680 on its own. The next two companies add less than half a point, and the other 72 companies together add 0.05. The total HHI is 9,680. Squaring is what makes the score so sensitive to one dominant company.

measure.title: From markets to one number per year
measure.takeaway: Our yearly measure: the share of the year's civilian contract dollars that sits in highly concentrated markets.
measure.notes: To follow 18 years, we need one number per year. We take every civilian segment, check its HHI, and add up the dollars in segments above 2,500. In FY2025 that is 152 billion dollars out of 301 billion, or 50 percent. That is the number we track from year to year.

methods.title: How we tested each finding
rows: Is the civilian rise real?
Shuffle (permutation) test
Would a trend this steep appear if the 18 years were in random order?
Where did the rise come from?
Decomposition
Split the change into each market's part. The parts add up exactly
Who holds the markets?
Ranking
The largest concentrated markets, and the company with the most money in each
Why did VA concentrate?
Case study and policy record
Follow one market, then match it to the laws and contracts
Was the money competed?
Breakdown by award type
Share of dollars competed against sole source
Is one market's rise real?
Per-market shuffle test
Does a market's rise beat its own shuffled years?
methods.takeaway: Every test asks one question: is the pattern bigger than what chance, or one big contract, would produce?
methods.notes: Each finding comes from a specific method. For the trend, a shuffle test, also called a permutation test: if the years were in random order, how often would we see a trend this steep? For where the rise came from, a decomposition that splits the change into each market's part, so the parts add up exactly to the total. For who, a ranking of the largest concentrated markets. For why, a case study of one market matched to the policy record. For competition, a breakdown of dollars by how they were awarded. And for single markets, the same shuffle idea applied to each market on its own. The next slides show each one.

finding1.title: Finding 1: the rise is real, and it is Veterans Affairs
finding1.takeaway: Civilian concentration rose from 44% to 50%, beyond chance. Take Veterans Affairs out and the rest is flat.
finding1.notes: How we tested it: we computed the yearly share, then how steep its trend is over 18 years. Then we shuffled the 18 yearly values into random order 20,000 times and measured the trend each time. If the real trend is steeper than almost all the shuffled ones, it is unlikely to be chance. The orange line is all civilian agencies: 44 percent in FY2008, 50 percent in FY2025, and only about 0.2 percent of shuffles are as steep, so the rise is real. The grey line is the same measure without Veterans Affairs. It goes from 45 to 42 percent, and about half of the shuffles are as steep, so there is no real trend. The rise in civilian concentration is almost entirely Veterans Affairs.
method: Compute each year's share (the yearly measure), then its trend
Shuffle the 18 years 20,000 times and refit the trend
Real if few shuffles are as steep. Redo without VA

finding2.title: Finding 2: a few markets drove it, not a broad shift
finding2.takeaway: Veterans Affairs added more than the whole rise. Thousands of other markets moved in and out of the band and roughly cancelled out.
finding2.notes: First, what the numbers mean. The civilian share, the yearly measure, was 40.5 percent in FY2012 to FY2014 and 47.8 percent in FY2023 to FY2025, a rise of 7.2 percentage points. We use 3-year windows so one big year cannot drive the result. Then we split those 7.2 points into the part each market contributed: its concentrated dollars as a share of all civilian dollars, then and now. The difference is that market's part, and all the parts add up exactly to 7.2. Adding the parts by agency gives this chart. Veterans Affairs added 11.6 points, more than the whole rise, because other agencies, led by NASA, took about 4 points away. And just 12 markets make up half of all the upward movement.
method: Compare FY2012 to FY2014 with FY2023 to FY2025
Each market: its concentrated $ ÷ all civilian $, then and now
The difference is its part. Add the parts by agency

finding3.title: Finding 3: who holds the concentrated markets
finding3.takeaway: Four of the six largest concentrated civilian markets are VA health care. McKesson's share is for distribution: the drugs come from many makers.
finding3.notes: These are the six largest highly concentrated civilian markets in FY2025, and the company with the largest share in each. The top three are all Veterans Affairs health care: UnitedHealth Group, through Optum, with 98 percent of managed healthcare; McKesson with 98 percent of drugs; and TriWest with all of government health insurance programs. One caution: McKesson is VA's drug distributor, so its share is for delivery, not for making the drugs, which come from many manufacturers.
method: Take the FY2025 civilian markets above 2,500
Name the company with the most money in each (its parent)

finding4.title: Finding 4: VA health care concentrated by design
facts: MISSION Act (June 2018) creates a permanent community care program
Network contracts competed: 3 bidders, fixed-price, Optum and TriWest win
Regions go live from Dec 2019 to Jun 2021
Claims pass through the administrator to community doctors
finding4.takeaway: VA chose to run community care through one administrator per region. The market concentrated by policy, through a competed contract.
finding4.notes: Why did VA managed healthcare concentrate? The 2018 MISSION Act created a permanent community care program. VA competed the Community Care Network contracts, three companies bid, and GAO denied a bid protest against the awards to Optum. The regions went live between December 2019 and June 2021, which is exactly when the money in our data jumps, from 389 million to over 22 billion dollars, and one company's share goes to 98 percent. The administrator pays community doctors and hospitals, so the money passes through it to many providers we do not see. GAO and VA's inspector general have both flagged oversight risks in these contracts.
method: Follow the top VA market year by year
Read the laws and GAO, VA and inspector general records
Match the dates to the jump in the data

finding5.title: Finding 5: concentrated, but competed
finding5.same: Concentrated civilian money was competed as often as the rest of civilian money.
finding5.exception: Mostly space research, where few organizations can do the work.
finding5.takeaway: Concentration mostly comes from competed contracts that give one winner the whole market, not from skipping competition.
finding5.notes: Is concentration a sign that agencies skip competition? Mostly not. In FY2025, 90 percent of the dollars in highly concentrated civilian markets were competed, the same as in all other markets. The pattern is competition for the market: one competition, then one winner for years. NASA is the exception, with over a third of its concentrated dollars sole source, mostly in space research.
method: Read each contract action's competition field
Group the dollars: competed or sole source
Compare concentrated markets with all the others

rising.title: What counts as a rising market?
rising.rule: Compare a market's average HHI in its last 3 years with its first 3 years. A gain of 500 points or more counts as rising: the rule in our proposal.
rising.why: Averaging 3 years softens one big contract. Single years still swing a lot, so the next slide tests each rise against chance.
rising.takeaway: A trend line follows one market for up to 18 years. Rising means its score climbed by at least 500 points.
rising.notes: Now we move from all civilian money to single markets. A trend line follows one market, one agency and one product, for up to 18 years. Here is VA managed healthcare. To call a market rising, our proposal compares the average score of its first three years with its last three. Here it went from 437 in FY2008 to FY2010 to 8,742 in FY2023 to FY2025, a gain of over 8,300 points, so it is clearly rising. Averaging three years softens the effect of one big contract, but scores still swing a lot from year to year.

lines.title: Is a market's rise real? The shuffle test
steps: Apply the rule to every market
A gain of 500+ points from the first 3 to the last 3 years
Keep its scores, mix their order, measure the gain again, 500 times. Rises here are luck
Keep rises that beat their shuffles
The real gain beats nearly all its shuffles, with a correction so at most 1 in 10 kept is luck
lines.takeaway: Most markets that pass the simple rule would pass by luck. The shuffle test keeps only the rises that are real.
lines.notes: Bar A: 54 percent of civilian markets pass the 500-point rule. Is that real? Bar B: we shuffled each market's yearly scores into random order, 500 times, and measured the gain again. Even in random order, 34 percent pass. So most of the markets in bar A could have passed by luck. Bar C: we keep a market only when its real gain beats nearly all of its own shuffles, with a standard correction, called Benjamini-Hochberg, so that at most about one in ten of the markets we keep is a false alarm. That leaves 22 percent of markets with a rise we can trust. This is the rule we will use from now on.

next.title: What it means, and what we do next
found: Half of civilian money is highly concentrated
The rise is real, and it is VA
careful: HHI shows the outcome, not why
Single years swing with big awards
steps: Group trend shapes, then ask what rising markets share
next.takeaway: Concentration in civilian contracting is real, focused in VA health care, and mostly chosen through competition. Next: what it costs.
next.notes: To sum up. Half of civilian contract money sits in highly concentrated markets. The rise is real, and it is almost entirely Veterans Affairs health care, which concentrated by policy through competed contracts. Keep in mind that our data shows the prime contractor only, that the score shows the outcome and not the reason, and that single years swing with big awards. Next we settle our data decisions with our sponsor, build the cleaned working set, group the trend shapes, and check subcontracts for the flagged markets. The open question for the rest of the project is what this concentration costs. Thank you.

backup_decisions.notes: These are the data decisions in plain words. Each issue, what we do about it, and why. They are the rules as proposed, and the team still has to confirm them. Together they change the concentration band of under 1 percent of markets.

backup_defense.title: Backup: Defense and civilian follow a similar path
backup_defense.notes: For context, Defense follows a similar path. Its FY2024 dip comes from combat ships and fixed-wing aircraft, which dropped below 2,500 that year and came back.

backup_kind.title: Backup: civilian services are where concentration grew
backup_kind.notes: Civilian services rose from 37 to 48 percent concentrated while service spending more than doubled. Research is highly concentrated throughout. Products barely moved.

backup_codes.title: Backup: product codes mostly carry across the code changes
backup_codes.note: The product code manuals changed in FY2012 and FY2021. Old codes were almost never retired. New codes were added and some spending moved onto them, mostly construction in FY2012 and IT in FY2021. So most markets can be followed for all 18 years.
backup_codes.notes: We worried that code changes would break our 18-year trend lines. They mostly do not.

backup_features.title: Backup: some fields change coverage over time
backup_features.note: The set-aside and offers fields go blank on many dollars from FY2018, mostly on orders under contract vehicles. The order competition field applies only to some orders, so it is blank on most dollars. These limits matter for explaining concentration later.
backup_features.notes: Sole source is stable at about a third of dollars. Two fields change coverage in FY2018.
